source.title: C$^{2}$R: Cross-sample Consistency Regularization Mitigates Feature Splitting and Absorption in Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Hao-Ran Jin; Xi-Ting Wang; Shijie Ren; Hong Xie; De-Fu Lian

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures splitting and absorption and argues that training objectives can encourage these pathologies, then tests a regularizer intended to mitigate them. It refines the claim rather than testing dictionary-size growth or cross-size feature correspondence.
record.gate_note: The paper reports Split Num and Absorption metrics across SAE methods, scales, regularization strengths, and backbones. It also reports reconstruction and other metrics, but those do not directly measure the claim. The authors' statements about results from cited studies were not recorded as results here. Figure 3 reports structural metrics across sparsity levels, but its values are plotted rather than tabulated.
record.test_reason: The study reports absorption and Split Num for unregularized SAEs (TopK, Batch TopK, AbsTopK) on Gemma-2-2B, Qwen3-8B and Llama-3-8B. It compares these with Matryoshka, OrtSAE and C2R objectives. It also argues formally that per-sample sparsity objectives favour splitting and absorption. This bears on V4 (absorption is present) and V6 (the objective drives these effects and changing it reduces them). There is no dictionary-size sweep, so V1, V3 and V5 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that C2R mitigates splitting and absorption while preserving reconstruction fidelity, interpretability and disentanglement. They claim a theoretical guarantee, which holds conditionally (88.1% of absorption pairs). They frame per-sample sparsity objectives as the root cause. They report Matryoshka scores lower on absorption and splitting but loses reconstruction fidelity, so C2R is best among fidelity-preserving methods.
record.recipe_differences: This study trains SAEs with a decoder-cosine-gated, batchwise activation-norm regularizer. It does not reproduce a dictionary-size sweep or track feature correspondences across dictionary sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with SAE backbone, model, layer, sparsity level, and C2R regularization strength. The study also reports seed variation for the Gemma-2-2B layer-12 setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Feature composition (mean max decoder cosine similarity) falls from about 0.33 (Batch TopK) to about 0.07–0.10 under C2R, and to 0.14–0.19 under Matryoshka, across models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE training objectives determine the redundancy (decoder overlap) of learned latents.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306 (2026)
record.problems: The theoretical guarantee is conditional and verified for 88.1% of absorption pairs. Most reported structural comparisons lack uncertainty estimates; the robustness table gives confidence intervals only for one setting. The 8B evaluations use one layer and one sparsity level, and no dictionary-size correspondence is tested. Some results in Figure 3 are plotted without tabulated values.
record.rows_left_out: To stay within the 60-row limit, omitted the separately reported structural metrics in Appendix G Tables 11–13 (Gemma-2-2B layer 20, 1B OpenWebText tokens, and The Pile) and the per-sparsity-level curves in Figure 3. Figure 3's narrative says C2R has the lowest splitting and absorption among methods preserving reconstruction fidelity, while Matryoshka has lower structural scores at a reconstruction cost; plotted values were not extracted as exact numbers.

untested.parts: Whole version: no dictionary-size sweep and no matching of coarse features to finer ones.
No splitting as the dictionary grows in the 8B models, and no open SAE releases. A single-size Split Num cannot show the pattern.
Whole version: no nested feature-family or hierarchy-geometry analysis.
Whether changing dictionary size fixes absorption. The sparsity sweep is only plotted (Figure 3).
Whether splitting says little about the model's own units. The causal role of correlated or hierarchical inputs is argued theoretically (Lemma 4.1), not shown empirically.

missing.what: Per-letter absorption rate vs feature frequency for 26 first-letter features in a Batch TopK SAE. Absorption reaches about 0.6 for some letters; Spearman ρ=+0.40.

record.verdict_notes: Split Num values sit near 1–1.35, i.e. little fragmentation at a fixed size of 65k latents. The record's V2 'supports' label is dropped because no dictionary-size scaling is shown. The record tied the Split Num rows to V4; they are re-linked to V6 only, since V4 names absorption. Lemma 4.1 (ℓ1 and TopK favour α→1) is a formal argument for V6's mechanism. Reductions in absorption often cost reconstruction: Matryoshka, λ=10, and the ablations (KL 0.84 for NoRCG). V6 does not claim the reductions are free, so this cost was not labelled.

versions.untested_parts: No dictionary-size sweep or matching of a smaller-dictionary feature to several larger-dictionary features; no test that those features cover the same inputs or lie near the smaller feature's direction.
The study measures splitting metrics on Qwen3-8B and Llama-3-8B, but does not test increasing dictionary sizes, compare corresponding features across sizes, or evaluate open SAE releases.
No nested feature-family analysis or test that feature families mirror a hierarchy of model concepts.

The study measures splitting and absorption metrics, including absorption defined by parent-latent failures when a child is present. It does not vary dictionary size. Its sparsity-level results are plotted rather than tabulated.
No cross-size decomposition of larger latents into smaller latents, and no test of whether larger dictionaries add novel latents.

The study compares splitting and absorption metrics across SAE objectives, backbones, and regularization strengths. It does not establish that the metrics are artifacts that say little about the model's own units, nor test correlated or hierarchical inputs as the cause.

source_check.notes: Sec 6.2 states each SAE has 65,536 latents. Tables 11-13 (Gemma L20, 1B tokens, Pile) show Split Num falling under every alternative objective. Single-run Split Num values are all multiples of 1/26 (1.1154 = 29/26), so it is a coarse metric. Table 8 BatchTopK Split Num is 1.0962 ± 0.0722 vs 1.1154 in Tables 14-15. Table 15 Split Num is non-monotonic in lambda: 1.0385 at 0.1 and 0.5, 1.1154 at 1.

statements.correction: Llama-3-8B layer 20, k=100 (Table 10): BatchTopK 0.1470; Matryoshka 0.0349; C2R 0.0410; OrtSAE 0.0979. Gemma-2-2B layer 12 (Table 8, 5 seeds): BatchTopK 0.1908 ± 0.0240 vs Matryoshka 0.0360 ± 0.0066.
statements.problem: The entry is about Matryoshka vs BatchTopK, but the Llama pair 0.035/0.041 has no labels. 0.041 is C2R, not Matryoshka.

statements.correction: Sec 6.2: each Gemma-2-2B layer 12 SAE has 65,536 latents (about 28x the residual dimension). App. E: Split Num (after Chanin et al. 2024) counts the minimum number of latents needed to improve a first-letter probe. Table 8 gives 5-seed means with 95% CIs.
statements.problem: The entry lists the 2606.30609 dictionary size as unknown, but the text gives it, and it matches 2503.17547's 65536. Split Num is also a latent count per first-letter concept, not a different kind of measure.

statements.correction: Split Num is unchanged only on Qwen3-8B (1.1154 for all methods). On Gemma L12 (Table 8) the changes stay within overlapping CIs. It drops on Llama-3-8B L20: 1.1923 to 1.0385 (OrtSAE, C2R) and 1.1154 (Matryoshka), Table 10. It drops on Gemma L12 TopK and AbsTopK backbones with C2R: 1.3462 to 1.0769, Table 16. It drops on Gemma L20: 1.3462 to 1.2308-1.2692, Table 11. It drops in the 1B-token and Pile runs: 1.1538 to 1.0385-1.0769, Tables 12-13. All are single runs.
statements.problem: It presents Qwen3-8B and Gemma Table 8 as the study's direct-splitting evidence. In the study's other settings, Split Num drops when the objective changes.

statements.correction: Split Num: Qwen3-8B 1.1154 for all methods. Gemma L12 Table 8: 1.0962 to 1.0385-1.0673, with overlapping CIs. Llama-3-8B: 1.1923 to 1.0385 (OrtSAE, C2R) or 1.1154 (Matryoshka). Gemma L12 TopK and AbsTopK backbones with C2R: 1.3462 to 1.0769. Gemma L20, 1B-token and Pile runs: lower under every alternative objective (Tables 11-13).
statements.problem: 'The direct splitting metric in 2606.30609 barely moves' holds only for Qwen3-8B and the Gemma L12 BatchTopK-based Table 8. V6.support[5] itself cites clear Split Num drops in the same study.

statements.correction: Split Num is flat on Qwen3-8B (1.1154) and within overlapping CIs on Gemma L12 (Table 8). It falls on Llama-3-8B from 1.1923 to 1.0385 (OrtSAE, C2R). On Gemma L12 TopK and AbsTopK backbones it falls from 1.3462 to 1.0769 with C2R. On Gemma L20, 1B-token and Pile runs it is lower under every alternative objective. All of these are single runs.
statements.problem: 'Yet the direct Split Num metric barely moves' is given as a summary of the whole study. It holds only for Qwen3-8B and Gemma L12 Table 8. The authors report that C2R mitigates splitting (Fig. 3b, Tables 10-13, 16).

reader_labels.reason: The reported splitting and absorption metrics vary across objective/backbone choices and with C2R strength; C2R often lowers them relative to its unregularized reference (rows t8-c2r-split, t8-c2r-abs, t14-c2r-split, t14-c2r-abs, t15-l5-abs, t16-topkc2r-split, t16-topkc2r-abs).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Matryoshka comparisons and strong C2R regularization
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that Matryoshka's lower splitting and absorption come at a reconstruction-fidelity cost, and that reconstruction begins degrading at λC2R=10; the structural metrics alone therefore do not establish a cost-free objective-based fix (rows t8-mat-split, t8-mat-abs, t15-l10-abs).
